utterances.text: And please, isn't it correct that in the document it is stated that during the battle, the 3rd Infantry Battalion Kravica, on the 7th of January, 1993, as it was retreating left behind the following materiel/technical means as follows: 60 mines -- MB 60-millimetre mines, 150 pieces; grenades, 20 pieces; automatic rifles, five pieces; machine-guns, M-53, ten pieces; rifles, 15 pieces; two anti-aircraft machine-guns. Now, could you please look at page 2 of this document. Isn't it true on this page under 24 it says: Weapons of fighters killed, in parenthesis, unverified, about 35 pieces?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Blouses, trousers, coats for 150 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it not say under item 3 that a three-barrel transporter from Bijeljina was destroyed, a four-barrel M-38, a ZIS, a B-1; six mortars?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, the gist of my question is: Are these not weapons which were used before this attack, during this attack against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Well, if the three-barrelled gun is from Bijeljina and the people from Bijeljina came to Kravica before Kravica fell a few days ago [as interpreted], how could this three-barrel piece have been used before if it arrived only a few days before Kravica burned down? How could it have been used before this event?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore you agree that soldiers from Bijeljina arrived to Kravica several days before the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Well, there's nothing to agree or not agree with I said that. This is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you also agree that there was a Kravica battalion there, the one that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you also agree that these units had their own weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that it's possible that these weapons were confiscated -- no, actually remained in Kravica, not confiscated. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It's possible. I would have to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I cannot tell you what I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like this document to be given an exhibit number and to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Registrar, please, that will be Defence Exhibit D40.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, there was an airport near Bratunac and Kravica. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far was the airport from Kravica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not an airport. These are fields. It's an airfield near Drina. I know about it, but it's not an airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Eric, that the Bratunac Brigade used four airplanes at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: I don't know. There weren't any where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You said that you returned to Kravica on the 17th or the 18th of March and that you found that everything was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, the 15th, the 16th, the 17th, is that something that is important?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You returned to Kravica in mid-March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the meantime, between the 7th of January and the 15th of March, you did not come back to Kravica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that you said that you didn't see what was going on during the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Except when I was on my way out, when I was leaving. That's what I described, that's what I saw. I didn't leave the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true then that you did not see what was going on in the period between January 7th and your return to Kravica in mid-March?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was deployed to a different battalion. So -- a battalion towards Voljevica because this one had fallen apart. So when it reformed, then I came back to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that the destruction that you found was something that could have been caused at any time and by anyone during those two months of your absence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: The question is not quite clear to me, but I think that all of this was destroyed on the 7th. If that's what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just told us that you did not see the attackers or what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Madam, in the conflict between Serbs and Muslims, who would be a third -- which would be a third party who could do something like that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just on the basis of the fact that there were no third parties, you are coming to the conclusion that --

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: No, of course not. We didn't attack ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So based on the fact that there was no third party, you draw this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Eric, isn't it true that there were major combat operations by Serb forces in this area known as the winter offensive?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Kravica was captured in fighting by numerous and different Serbian forces in the middle of March?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I know that. I took part in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you took part in that battle?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. I am proud of that. I took part in the capture of my own village. There's nothing in dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please place on the ELMO document of the command of the Zvornik Brigade of the 14th of March, 1993, number 00808449, combat order number 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like the witness to refrain from swearing. Could you please look at item 3 which says: “The combined armoured detachment grouping the main forces attacks the road section in the direction Konjevic Polje, Lolici, Kravica, and auxiliary forces (detachment north supported by a tank destroyer and an armoured APC)."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I would like to ask you something. Is a self-propelled weapon a destructive artillery weapon?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is an armoured transporter the same thing?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: Yes. An armoured transporter is less destructive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it is destructive?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that combined armoured units or companies took part in this battles?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Eric, then it is possible that these weapons were the ones which inflicted the damage that you talked about in your testimony, isn't that so, during the recapture of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like this document to be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be Defence Exhibit D41. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: {Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, now I would like to ask you just a few more short questions. You said that your late grandfather was Golub Eric?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His brother is Nego Eric?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: Negoslav Eric called Nego.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that both of them were killed in this fight on the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: No. Golub was killed earlier and Nego was killed on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nego Eric is your uncle? He's the brother of your grandfather?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: Yes, his brother is Golub.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was he during this attack?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: He was born in 1911, so he was about 70-plus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that he died firing at Muslims, shooting at Muslims?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in the process he killed his own wife, Kristina, and then he killed himself?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: We are assuming that, but I don't know exactly because she was burned and my grandfather had a bullet through his mouth. So he probably shot her and then killed himself later, but he did fire at Muslim fighters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your grandfather and his brother following World War II were sentenced to a long prison sentence because of a massacre of 86 Muslims from the village of Sopotnik?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: They were sentenced to death by execution, but you have to let me say something else. If you mentioned World War II, you must allow me, and I need to ask the Judges' permission for me to say something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you to reply to my question, whether it's true that they were sentenced.

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. But may I say something?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is a part of the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, you answer the question and that's it. We don't want to hear more about these events. Madam Vidovic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1995 between 1.000 and 1500 Muslims were killed in the village of Kravica. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your close cousins Zoran Eric participate in the killings of hundreds of these Muslims?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: No. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you, Mr. Eric?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: I was in Trnovo, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you claim that you were not in this area, that you were not in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I have proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Madam Vidovic. Is there re-examination, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Re-examined by Ms. Sellers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, you stated that -- you testified in response to the Defence counsel question that your grandfather died while shooting at Muslims. Was he shooting at Muslims during the attack in his village in Kravica on the 7th January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: No, no. When they attacked the house, when they attacked the house itself, when they reached the house, then he fired from the house at them. He wasn't on the lines of defence; he was in the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it if he was born in 1911 and these events happened in 1993, he was 82, 81, 82 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree. And that's precisely my point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he shooting at Muslim forces in order to defend his house in Kravica as it was under attack?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question. And Mr. Eric, you testified that to your knowledge that you thought that Mr. Naser Oric might have been the commander of the Bosnian Muslim forces. My question is: Did you receive --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if that's a correct statement of his evidence. There was very conflicting evidence. He said he had no reliable information. He said he didn't know -- in fact, in cross-examination, if we review the transcript that was not -- that was not his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's precisely why I am rising -- I'm raising it, how it was characterised in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go on and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If it's a non-leading question, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm merely trying to retrace -- I thank counsel for his correction. I'm trying to retrace how it was phrased on direct examination. He said to your knowledge. I wanted to ask you:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that knowledge come from television or papers or any other source?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Actually, it wasn't important to us who the commander of the Muslim forces was. We were busy with our own troubles to defend our village. And this about Naser Oric is something that we heard from television, radio, it was something that was talked about. But we -- it doesn't matter who it was. We were not interested specifically in who it was. We didn't have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers. Judge Brydensholt would like to put a question to you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: You have explained that this village guard changed around November 1992 and became part of the army, as far as I understood. Does that mean that they got uniforms? I can see that about uniforms for 150 soldiers were left on the 7th of January. So was this guard uniformed at the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: No. For example, I personally on January 7th was wearing civilian clothes. I had a shirt which was part of the uniform of the former JNA. People did have pieces of uniform, but the unit as a whole was not kitted out and dressed in uniform. People had pieces of that military uniform. And you can see that in the photographs when those people were found, when Dr. Stankovic was making those photographs, you could see that some people were wearing those olive-drab uniforms of the former JNA. And they were probably left to us by people when the army was withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And what about the weapons? I can see that quite a number of weapons, also heavy weapons, were left behind on the 7th of January. Was that kind of weapon also given to the village guard members?

utterances.speaker: Again, the Zvornik Brigade…the fuckin’ Zvornik brigade…
utterances.text: No. This was left -- it was located in the centre of the village and then when a position was attacked or jeopardised, then the weapon was deployed. But I don't know exactly how it was deployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Brydensholt. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Before I put a question to the witness, I would like to ask -- pose of Defence and the Prosecution, as it had been before with other witnesses there are -- had been references to a book "The Bloody Christmas in the Village of Kravica." Now I wanted to ask whether this book is to be considered as a reliable report and whether the Prosecution at any point would challenge this or whether -- would you agree with regard to the proper value of this book?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position on that, and we know that the Defence has with other witnesses used portions of this book and I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. believe you can see from the testimony those witnesses gave, a couple of the witnesses didn't agree with what was written, didn't recognise it. I believe my colleague had raised objections in terms of the relevance materiality. This witness had portions of it read out, he listened to it. He didn't necessarily agree with all the characterisation. Your Honour, I think the Prosecution's point on this would be since we do understand the Trial Chamber would prefer to see things, to look at them, to weigh for themselves, that we're objecting to its admission when the Defence tenders it, but what we would be arguing is that the weight given to this book must be closely examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I may add something on this point, we are also unaware whether the Defence that has been relying on excerpts from this book as pieces of evidence intends to bring forward the author as one of the witnesses. We don't know that. Because it does of course make a difference if he makes himself available. Anyway, I don't think at this point in time we should, knowing that the Prosecution itself is not contesting the admissibility of this document, I think we can leave it at that for the time being. And we'll consider the value, if any, to give to this book later on, if necessary. But yes, Madam Vidovic, do you have anything to say in regard?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, regarding what is written in this book, we are asking questions. Other than that, we will bring other evidence in relation to that book, documents, facts, and other evidence, witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So even if you use other evidence, at any rate you used this book as a sort of indirect way of contrasting witnesses. And I must say that it's not very easy for the Trial Chamber to be left in the air, both by the Defence and by the Prosecution with regard to the reliability of this book. I personally would be quite happy to know how books which are introduced in the evidence procedure are to be looked upon, as reliable or less reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just to add one perspective. As my colleague said, it's a source of propositions which are being put to witnesses. And to the extent they adopt those propositions or to the extent those propositions are corroborated by other evidence, then we would submit that that's a probative value. We are not at this stage seeking to rely on the book itself as providing evidence. That's a matter which we may see again in due course, however.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. In light of what counsel has stated, do I understand that possibly Defence counsel would be withdrawing the book from admission into evidence at this time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to complicate it thus far. I think the only legal way of approaching this issue as it stands to date is that the book itself is not sworn testimony; it's just information that is being used by the Defence so far. Either -- we don't have an indication that it's going to be used by you as well but you are free to do so. And the information contained in that book is being put to the various witnesses, and they required or requested to answer whether they agree or disagree with the content of -- the contents of the part usually they are referred to. What becomes evidence is their answer and not the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have a similar situation with the newspaper article which was introduced by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the same if you read our decision in the Brdjanin judgement. You will see that it is wrong even to submit that newspaper articles are testimony. They are not testimony. That was submitted in that case that they were testimony heard under Rule 92 bis, which is -- couldn't be farther from the truth. But anyway, let's not meander and get lost on this. The book is not being considered, at least for the time being, as evidence that you are bringing forward. It's being considered to be a piece of evidence in the sense that it's tendered in evidence but not as proof of its own content. In other words, what is relevant is what the witnesses are answering in relation to those excerpts and not the book itself. Otherwise, without the author coming forward to confirm the contents, I mean, we get nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. And if a hundred witnesses were to confirm a portion of the book, then the book itself might assume some probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. We would still -- we would still not need to go into that merit, because if you have a hundred witnesses confirming the contents of that book, you rely on the hundred witnesses and you don't need to rely on the book. So, Mr. Eric, that brings us to the end of your testimony. I wish to -- before you leave the courtroom, I wish to thank you, that's on my own behalf and also on behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, but also on behalf of the Tribunal in general. We wish to thank you for having accepted to come over and give evidence in this trial. You will be escorted by Madam Usher out of this courtroom and then you will receive all the assistance that you require to enable you to return home to your work and to your family. Last but not least, we all wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I wish to thank the Prosecution and Defence for having cooperated together and managed to succeed at completing the testimony of this witness within a day, as agreed. Tomorrow we will be sitting in the morning and not in the afternoon. And we will be sitting in Courtroom II and not in Courtroom I like today. It may be smaller, but at least we will have the advantage of finishing in the morning and early afternoon and not late in the evening. The same should apply on Thursday. Now, next witness. You had indicated three hours to us. So what's the position, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution would like to limit the time until around two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two hours. And Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think an hour and a half would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you should plan to finish with this witness tomorrow? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow will be Wednesday. And then Thursday the important thing is it seems it could be done, because the next two witnesses, number 4 and number 5, are all scheduled to have two hours. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The same applies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. What we would like you to do is to ensure that these two witnesses will also be gone from The Hague by the end of the week. Okay. I thank you so much. Once more we have stayed a little bit longer. Technicians, interpreters, and everyone else, I would like to thank you on behalf of my colleagues and myself for having stayed with us for a few more minutes. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of October, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
